Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

lowercase rough brief: can you organize this into a prompt for writing an email to the chess tournament director? I need the result to be an email body, not an email that you send, and the point is to make a registration request without acting like we already know the director’s answer. It should be courteous and fairly concise for an event organizer who is handling a lot of entries, but include enough concrete information that Dana can identify the player and the event without having to ask which tournament I mean. The event is the Cedar Bridge Open, run by the Cedar Bridge Chess Club at the Westfield Public Library on May 18. It is a one-day, five-round Swiss tournament, with rounds scheduled at 9:00 a.m., 11:00 a.m., 1:00 p.m., 3:00 p.m., and 5:00 p.m. The registration contact is Dana Holt. I have not heard directly from Dana, and there is no confirmation of an entry yet.

The main request has to depend on the registration status. If the U1600 section is still accepting entries when the email is handled, ask Dana to register Rowan Bell in that section. That is the primary request, but it is allowed only while registration is open; don’t make it sound like Rowan is already entered or that a place has been held. If the section has closed, the different request should be to add Rowan to the U1600 waitlist and let Rowan know if a place becomes available. Don’t ask to switch to the Open section as the backup, since Rowan wants the U1600 section, and don’t make both requests as if they apply at once. We don’t know which status is true, so make the wording conditional rather than guessing. Rowan would rather have a clear answer about the waitlist than receive a general message about other tournaments.

Player details to include are Rowan Bell, US Chess membership number 14590327, current published rating 1486, and the U1600 section preference. Rowan has an active US Chess membership, so don’t ask whether membership is current or suggest that a new membership is needed. The rating is the published rating Rowan is using for this request; don’t round it, call it provisional, or describe it as a tournament result. There is no need to say how long Rowan has played chess or add biographical background. Rowan has played at the library once before, but that is not relevant to the registration and does not need to go in the email. The email should be from Rowan, in first person, not written as if a parent, coach, or club representative is contacting Dana on Rowan’s behalf.

The posted event information gives an entry fee of $45. Rowan has not paid it, and no payment has been made or attached to this email. If the section is still open, ask Dana how Rowan should pay the fee after the entry is accepted; don’t claim payment is enclosed, don’t offer card details, and don’t ask Dana to waive the fee. There is a note on the club page from a volunteer that says, “We are still checking the room count, so please ask before sending payment.” Keep that quotation exactly as written if it is included, and use it only as context for asking about the next payment step; it is not a confirmation that the tournament is full or that registration has closed. I think it makes sense to mention that Rowan saw the note, but don’t turn the email into a complaint about unclear instructions.

For organization, it may help to make the decision point easy to scan, since Dana should be able to see the requested action immediately. One numbered section would be fine if it feels natural, perhaps separating the registration condition from the identifying details, but don’t force a long form or turn the email into a checklist. It should read like a real, brief message from a player to an organizer. Mention the date and venue so the event is unambiguous, but there is no need to recite the full round schedule unless it helps identify the event. I included the schedule here so the event details are clear, not because Rowan needs to ask about start times, pairing rules, parking, or library access. Don’t invent any of those details or add questions about them.

Rowan plans to attend if an entry is available and can be reached at rowan.bell@example.com. The email should not imply that travel has been booked or that Rowan needs special arrangements. A simple greeting to Dana and a polite closing signed Rowan are appropriate. Keep the tone friendly and direct rather than overly formal, apologetic, or urgent. The status is unknown, so do not guess or suggest that the event is full.
